extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy; policymakers and advocates concerned with civil liberty and limits of social/governmental coercion
extracted.subtask_description: Principled guidance on when society or government may legitimately interfere with individual action (the 'harm principle'), and related limits on coercion, freedom of thought, expression, tastes, and association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm Principle (sole end of interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power may be rightfully exercised over a member of society only "to prevent harm to others." The good of the agent (physical or moral), or what makes him happier or wiser, is not a sufficient warrant for compulsion; such reasons justify persuasion but not coercion. This principle governs both legal penalties and moral coercion of public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: Applicability only to mature persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine applies "only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children and persons legally deemed immature may be legitimately subject to protective compulsion. Similarly, in 'backward states of society' where the race is in nonage, despotism may be legitimate if aimed at improvement and actually effective. Liberty as a principle requires capacity for improvement by free discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere of individual liberty — inward domain of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The inward domain of consciousness; demanding liberty of conscience, in the most comprehensive sense; liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This domain is described as directly and primarily concerning only the individual; it entails absolute freedom of thought, feeling, and conscience. The liberty of expressing and publishing opinions is practically inseparable from liberty of thought because of their importance and common foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere of individual liberty — tastes and pursuits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like, subject to such consequences as may follow... so long as what we do does not harm [others], even though they should think our conduct foolish, perverse, or wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals may shape and live their lives according to personal character and preferences without interference so long as they do not harm others. Social disapproval or perceptions of foolishness are not legitimate grounds for compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere of individual liberty — freedom of association
rubrics_metrics.description: "The liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite, for any purpose not involving harm to others: the persons combining being supposed to be of full age, and not forced or deceived."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons of full age may freely associate for any lawful purpose that does not harm others; associations obtained by force, deception, or involving harm fall outside this liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against social tyranny (opinion as coercion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society can "execute its own mandates" and "practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection must extend beyond legal limits to include safeguards against coercion by prevailing opinion and feeling. Social pressure can penetrate the details of life and constrain individuality; thus limits on collective moral coercion are as essential as protection against magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that interference be justified by preventing others' harm, not by agent's own good
rubrics_metrics.description: "His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant... These are good reasons for remonstrating with him... but not for compelling him... To justify that, the conduct from which it is desired to deter him must be calculated to produce evil to some one else."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsion must be tied to the prevention of externally directed harm. Activities thought beneficial for the actor or socially desirable cannot be mandated solely for that reason; they may warrant persuasion but not legal or moral coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for actions vs. omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: "A person may cause evil to others not only by his actions but by his inaction... To make any one answerable for doing evil to others, is the rule; to make him answerable for not preventing evil, is, comparatively speaking, the exception."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society may justifiably hold individuals responsible for harmful actions. Holding them responsible for failing to prevent harm requires greater caution and is an exception justified only in clear and grave cases. Where compulsion is not applied, individual conscience should guard others' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible legal compulsion for certain positive duties
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many positive acts for the benefit of others which he may rightfully be compelled to perform; such as, to give evidence in a court of justice; to bear his fair share in the common defence... and to perform certain acts of individual beneficence, such as saving a fellow-creature's life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While private conduct is largely immune from coercion, society legitimately compels certain duties directly related to external relations and common interests (e.g., court testimony, defense, rescue) when clearly necessary for others' welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of discussion as safeguard for truth and correction of error
rubrics_metrics.description: "The peculiar evil of silencing the expression of an opinion is, that it is robbing the human race... If the opinion is right, they are deprived of the opportunity of exchanging error for truth: if wrong, they lose... the clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silencing opinions assumes infallibility. Discussion and the open contest of ideas are essential because human judgment is corrigible only when challenged; free discourse is the chief mechanism by which truth is approached and errors corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument against silencing opinions: assumption of infallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbidding an opinion presumes that those who forbid it are absolutely certain and infallible. Given human fallibility and historical reversals of consensus, the state or society lacks authority to exclude dissenting opinion from hearing and contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of keeping avenues open to criticism to sustain justified conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: The beliefs we have most warrant for "have no safeguard to rest on, but a standing invitation to the whole world to prove them unfounded... The beliefs which we have most warrant for, have no safeguard to rest on, but a standing invitation to the whole world to prove them unfounded."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable confidence in one's convictions requires exposure to criticism. Those whose judgments are to be trusted have arrived at them by listening to contrary arguments; the public should be required to maintain open forums for challenge if it wishes to claim justified convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on government interference determined more by principle than preference
rubrics_metrics.description: There is "a limit to the legitimate interference of collective opinion with individual independence" and currently "there is no recognised principle by which the propriety or impropriety of government interference is customarily tested. People decide according to their personal preferences."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about government intervention should not rest on shifting preferences or partisan inclination; instead, a consistent principle (such as the harm principle) should determine when interference is proper. Absent such principle, both overreach and undue abstention are common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility as ultimate ethical appeal grounded in permanent human interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The author "forego[es] any advantage... from the idea of abstract right... I regard utility as the ultimate appeal on all ethical questions; but it must be utility in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and legal limits on liberty are defended on utilitarian grounds—promoting the long-term, progressive interests of humanity. This frames the harm principle: interference is permissible insofar as it protects others' interests necessary for a progressive social order.
